query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation of a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is primarily caused by the synergistic effects of solid-solution strengthening, refined grain structures, and precipitation hardening induced by the σ phase enriched with Fe, Cr, and Mo.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature, simultaneous wear and corrosion
generation.structural_mediator: σ phase enriched with Fe, Cr, and Mo
generation.mechanism: Synergistic effects of solid-solution strengthening, refined grain structures, and precipitation hardening
generation.baseline: Single-phase FCC structure without σ phase
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 500-700°C, wear rate: 10^-4 - 10^-3 mm^3/N·m, corrosion current density: 10^-6 - 10^-5 A/cm^2
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of σ phase formation and its effect on the degradation process is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with and without σ phase under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate and corrosion current density of the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with σ phase are not significantly higher than those of the alloy without σ phase, then the hypothesis is falsified

As shown in Figure 1, among these, laser cladding has demonstrated unique advantages through its high energy density (typically 103–104 W/mm2) and rapid cooling rates (103–106 K/s), enabling the fabrication of coatings with superior characteristics: low dilution rates, narrow heat-affected zones (HAZ < 200 μm), and excellent metallurgical bonding (interface strength > 400 MPa) []. These attributes have rendered it particularly advantageous for critical applications in marine engineering and precision machinery manufacturing.
Current research in laser cladding coating fabrication predominantly employs a two-stage methodology: initial powder preplacement onto the substrate surface, followed by laser irradiation to achieve simultaneous fusion of the deposited material with the base substrate, thereby forming high-quality coatings. Zhang et al. [] synthesized CoCrFeNiTi HEA coatings on 304SS via laser cladding using ball-milled pre-alloyed powders. Currently, most research on laser cladding HEA coatings focuses on pre-coating the substrate with powder, followed by scanning with a high-energy laser beam to form the coating, but this method relies on the use of organic solvents. This can lead to the formation of pores and the introduction of impurities during the cooling process of the laser melt pool. In contrast, coaxial powder-fed laser cladding technology is suitable for surfaces with complex geometries and allows for precise control of the cladding area without the need for binders. This eliminates issues related to porosity and impurities while offering broader application potential.
The transition metal elements Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni are conventionally selected as primary constituents of HEAs due to their comparable atomic radii. ## 2.1. Coating Deposition
The experimental platform employed Q355 steel substrates (100 mm × 100 mm × 20 mm). The Q355 steel used complies with ATSM A992 [], and the quantitative characterization of its elemental composition is shown in Table 1. As the cladding material, CoCrFeNiMo HEA powder was procured from Avimetal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). The physical appearance of the HEA powder is depicted in Figure 2b.
As shown in Figure 3, laser deposition was executed via a LYR3063 system (LYR3063, Jinan Senfeng Technology Co., Ltd., Jinan, China) under four distinct power configurations: 1750, 2000, 2250, and 2500 W. Other process parameters were standardized as follows: 150 cm/min scanning velocity, 1.5 rpm powder feed rate, 2 mm beam diameter, and 50% overlap ratio with 1 mm/pass advancement.
